```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE)
```

##Introduction

For this project we used the "what we watched on Netflix" dataset from TidyTuesday(week of July 29,2025).Netflix releases a report every six months that shows how many hours people spent watching each movie and show.We put four of these reports together so our data covers the second half of 2023 to the first half of 2025.

The data comes in two files,one for movies and one for shows and both have the same eight columns.These include the title,the report period,the release date on Netflix,whether the title was available globally,the hours viewed and the runtime.There is also a views column,which is hours viewed divided by runtime,so it is a rough count of how many times a title was watched.Each row is one title in one report so the same title can show up more than once. 

##Question 1:Does Newer content Get More Views on Netflix?

##Introduction
Our first question was whether newer movies and shows get more views than older ones.We were curious about this because newer titles might get more attention,especially when Netflix promotes them.To answer it we used the release date and the report period to find how old each title was and then compared the age to views.Since a few titles have very large numbers of views we used a log scale.We also looked at movies and shows separately.

## Question 1 Approach

We use a scatter plot to present the relationship between content age on Netflix and views. This plot is suitable because it can display two numerical variables and allows us to identify patterns in the data. We also add a smooth trend line to show the relationship and use facets to compare movies and shows separately.

For the second plot, we use a point-range plot to compare views across different content age groups. This plot is suitable because it presents each group’s viewing performance and variability. It is easier to compare differences between age groups. We use the median to represent typical views and the interquartile range to show the spread of the observations. We also use facets to separate movies and shows.

## Question 1 Analysis

```{r Question1 Analysis, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
# install.packages("ggplot2")
# install.packages("tidyverse")
# install.packages("scales")
library(ggplot2)
library(tidyverse)
library(scales)

# Load the datasets.
movies <- readr::read_csv('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/main/data/2025/2025-07-29/movies.csv')
shows <- readr::read_csv('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/main/data/2025/2025-07-29/shows.csv')

# Combine the movies and shows datasets and remove missing release_date values.
q1_netflix <- bind_rows(
  movies %>% 
    mutate(content_type = "Movie") %>% 
    filter(!is.na(release_date)),
  shows %>% 
    mutate(content_type = "Show") %>% 
    filter(!is.na(release_date))
)

# Convert release_date to Date format and use the end date of each reporting period to calculate the content's age on Netflix. 
# Calculate the age by subtracting release_date from report_end_date, then convert it to years for easier interpretation on the x-axis.
q1_netflix <- q1_netflix %>%
  mutate(
    release_date = as.Date(release_date),
    
    # Create a column for the end date of each reporting period. Keep the first four characters (the year) and replace the remaining part with the corresponding end date.
    report_end_date = case_when(
      str_detect(report, "Jan-Jun") ~
        as.Date(paste0(str_sub(report, 1, 4), "-06-30")), 
      str_detect(report, "Jul-Dec") ~
        as.Date(paste0(str_sub(report, 1, 4), "-12-31"))
      ),
    content_netflix_age_days =
      as.numeric(report_end_date - release_date),
    content_netflix_age =
      content_netflix_age_days / 365
  )
```

```{r Question1 Figure1, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
ggplot(
  q1_netflix,
  aes(x = content_netflix_age,
      y = views
     )
) +
  geom_point(
    alpha = 0.15,
    size = 0.6
  ) +
  
  # Add a smooth trend line to show the relationship between content age and views.
  # se = FALSE removes the confidence interval shading.
  geom_smooth( 
    se = FALSE
  ) +
  
  # Create separate panels for movies and shows.
  facet_grid(
    . ~ content_type
  ) +
  
  # Use a base-10 logarithmic scale for the y-axis and display values with commas.
  scale_y_log10(
    labels = label_comma()
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Relationship Between Netflix Content Age and Views",
    x = "Years Since Netflix Release",
    y = "Views (log scale)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r Question1 Figure2, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
# Group views by content age to compare viewing performance across age groups.
age_summary_2 <- q1_netflix %>%
  
  # Keep records with valid content age and positive views.
  filter(
    content_netflix_age >= 0,
    views > 0
  ) %>%
  
  # Divide content into age groups based on years since Netflix release.
  mutate(
    age_group = cut(
      content_netflix_age,
      
      # Define the boundaries for each age group.'Inf' represents positive infinity, allowing the last group to include all values greater than or equal to 10.
      breaks = c(0, 1, 3, 5, 10, Inf),
      
      # Exclude the right boundary of each interval.
      right = FALSE,
      labels = c(
        "<1 year",
        "1-<3 years",
        "3-<5 years",
        "5-<10 years",
        "10+ years"
      )
    )
  ) %>%
  
  # Group records by content type and age group.
  group_by(content_type, age_group) %>%
  
  # Calculate the number of records, median views, and the 25th and 75th percentiles.
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    median_views = median(views),
    q25 = quantile(views, 0.25),
    q75 = quantile(views, 0.75),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# Plot the median views as points and use vertical lines to show the interquartile range.
ggplot(
  age_summary_2,
  aes(
    x = age_group,
    y = median_views
  )
) +
  geom_pointrange(
    aes(
      ymin = q25, # Set the lower end of the range to the 25th percentile.
      ymax = q75  # Set the upper end of the range to the 75th percentile.
    )
  ) +
  
  # Create separate panels for movies and shows.
  facet_grid(. ~ content_type) +
  
  # Customize the x-axis labels and add line breaks to improve readability.
  scale_x_discrete(
      labels = c(
        "<1 year",
        "1-<3\nyears",
        "3-<5\nyears",
        "5-<10\nyears",
        "10+ years"
      )
  ) + 
  
  # Use a base-10 logarithmic scale for the y-axis and display values with commas.
  scale_y_log10(
    labels = label_comma()
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Median Views by Time Since Netflix Release",
    x = "Years Since Netflix Release",
    y = "Views (log scale)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

##Discussion
Overall the plots support our hypothesis that newer content gets more views.In figure 1 the trend lines for both movies and shows drop quickly in the first two to three years.Figure 2 shows the same pattern.The median for movies in the 0 to 1 year group is around 5 million views and it goes down to about 100,000 for movies that are 10 or more years old.

Shows are a little different at the older end.Their trend line flattens after about three years and then goes up after about 10 years and the 10+ year median is higher than the 3 to 10 year medians.This might be because only a few very old shows are still on Netflix and those are probably popular ones that people like to rewatch.Still we cannot say from these figures alone that older shows get more views than older movies.

We removed the rows with missing release_date values which left about 6,700 movies and 13,700 shows.Both figures have fewer points for titles older than 10 years,so the lines in that range may be strongly affected by a small number of observations.This makes the rise in the show trend line less reliable.

Another limit is that age here means the time since the Netflix release not the original release.An older movie that only recently came to Netflix would count as new which might change the results.So newer content does get more views in general but the pattern for older titles is less clear.

##Question 2:Does Global Availability Lead to More Views?

##Introduction
Our second question was whether titles that are available globally get more views than titles that are only available in some regions.People usually know whether something is on Netflix but they may not think about where it is available.A global title can reach a much bigger audience so we expected it to get more views.To test this we split the titles into two groups using the available_globally column and compared their views on a log scale.We made separate plots for movies and shows.

## Question 2 Approach

For the first plot, we have created a ridge plot for a cursory look at the frequency of view counts across shows and movies on Netflix that are either globally available or region-locked. This plot enables us to find immediate patterns in the distribution of views that shows and movies get based on if the content is available globally or not.

For the second plot, we take a closer look at the viewcounts via violin box plot. This way we can directly compare viewcounts between globally available and region-locked shows and movies via measures of central tendency such as median while still retaining an idea of the distributions that each category displays.

## Question 2 Analysis
```{r Question2 Analysis, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
#install.packages("tidytuesdayR")
#install.packages("ggplot2")
#install.packages("scales")
#install.packages("tidyverse")
#install.packages("ggridges")
library(ggridges)
library(tidyverse)
library(scales)
library(ggplot2)
library(tidytuesdayR)

# Load datasets
tuesdata <- tidytuesdayR::tt_load('2025-07-29')
movies <- tuesdata$movies
shows <- tuesdata$shows

# Remove entries with missing viewcount and global availability data
movies_clean <- movies %>%
  filter(!is.na(available_globally)) %>%
  filter(!is.na(views))

shows_clean <- shows %>%
  filter(!is.na(available_globally)) %>%
  filter(!is.na(views))

# Combine movie and show datasets
q2_netflix <- bind_rows(
  movies_clean %>% 
    mutate(content_type = "Movie"),
  shows_clean %>% 
    mutate(content_type = "Show"))
```

```{r Question2 Figure1, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
ggplot(q2_netflix,
       aes(x = views,
           y = available_globally,
           fill = available_globally)) +
  # Display view axis values using log-10 scale and change from scientific notation to commas
  scale_x_log10(labels = label_comma()) +
  geom_density_ridges(alpha = 0.5) +
  guides(fill = "none") +
  # Separate movies and shows into different graphs
  facet_grid( . ~ content_type) +
  labs(
    title = "Frequency of Viewcounts for Globally Available and Region-locked Movies and Shows on Netflix",
    x = "Views (log scale)",
    y = "Global Availability"
  )
```

```{r Question2 Figure2, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
ggplot(q2_netflix,
       aes(x = available_globally,
           y = views)) +
  # Display view axis values using log-10 scale and change from scientific notation to commas
  scale_y_log10(labels = label_comma()) +
  geom_violin(fill = "green3") +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.05) +
  # Separate movies and shows into different graphs
  facet_grid( . ~ content_type) +
  labs(
    title = "Comparison of Viewcounts for Globally Available and Region-locked Movies and Shows on Netflix",
    x = "Global Availability",
    y = "Views (log scale)"
  )
```

##Discussion
The plots support our hypothesis.In Figure 1 the median views for globally available movies is around 700,000 compared to about 200,000 for regional movies.Figure 2 looks similar with a median of about 800,000 for global shows and about 300,000 for regional shows.In both figures the box for global titles sits higher than the box for regional titles.

The regional groups also have a lot of titles near the bottom of the scale around 100,000 views.This is the long flat part on the left violin in each plot.Even so some regional titles still reach very high views and the outliers in the regional movie group go up to tens of millions.So being regional does not mean a title cannot do well it just makes it less likely.

We need to be careful about saying global availability is the cause.Global titles may also be the ones Netflix promotes the most such as its own originals so promotion could explain part of the difference.Each title can also appear in more than one report so the observations are not fully independent.The two groups may not be the same size either so a smaller group could look different just because it has fewer points.So global titles do get more views in general but these figures alone cannot tell us why.
